title: Give me 24 mins. I'll teach you how to conquer rejection (by AI CEO David Shim)
guest: David Shim, co-founder and CEO of Read AI, former CEO of Foursquare, founder of Placed (sold to Snapchat for $200M)
summary: In a Season 3 conference interview, David Shim traces his hustler upbringing from selling hand-drawn Desert Storm cards in elementary school to selling Placed to Snapchat for $200M, and shares his philosophy on rejection, sales, public speaking, competition and the future of AI. The sisters then debrief on the takeaways: forget rejections quickly, treat investor questions as a feature roadmap, let feedback wash off you, and view competitors as free market education.

ideas.idea: Just reach out to people; no one cares that you contacted them and they will probably forget, so there is no downside to outreach.
ideas.detail: David credits the My First Million podcast for this day-to-day advice and links it to 'failure training' from selling newspapers door to door and recruiting for his fraternity.

ideas.idea: You won't find product-market fit until you've been rejected a dozen times or more, so rejection is a built-in part of founding.
ideas.detail: David frames finding customers and product-market fit as a rejection-heavy process he was trained for by early sales jobs.

ideas.idea: An entrepreneurial mindset is built by early childhood work and immigrant-family hustle, where more hours reliably means more money.
ideas.detail: From age six David shopped at Costco and stocked his mom's deli (learning to turn Coke cans label-forward); his father sold cars with limited English; at 11-12 he delivered newspapers with his mom driving because he was too scrawny to bike.

ideas.idea: Start a business with whatever resources you have, even library printers and hand drawings; the key is near-zero input cost.
ideas.detail: In elementary school David hand-drew Desert Storm trading cards, printed them on library computers (getting shut down for the $0.50/page cost), wrapped them with candy and sold them for $1-2 each, then moved to selling candy at school.

ideas.idea: Don't set out to 'be an entrepreneur'; instead notice a specific problem nobody is working on and build for it.
ideas.detail: Placed began when David saw no one was converting smartphone location data into store visits; it grew to measuring a few billion dollars of annual advertising before Snap acquired it.

ideas.idea: Break the rules within the law: Read AI broke the assumption that everyone should be in meetings by measuring real-time engagement.
ideas.detail: An LLM summarizing a pitch would say 'great meeting', but tracking whether 20 people on a call are paying attention reveals a bad meeting, which is useful because it tells you to have fewer of them or to pivot in real time.

ideas.idea: If you want to build something great, throw yourself entirely into your work; work-life balance is not how Google, Snapchat or nuclear energy got built.
ideas.detail: Advice to his 29- and 35-year-old selves: make major sacrifices to find out quickly whether your idea works rather than spending four more years at nine-to-five pace; you'll only regret not going all in.

ideas.idea: Seeing people respond to your vision feels better than almost anything else in the world.
ideas.detail: David and Jean describe being in a flow state working every day and weekend when passionate about what they're building.

ideas.idea: The philosophy of selling is to forget quickly: log what didn't work, iterate the pitch, and never let a few rejections kill the idea.
ideas.detail: Placed was rejected in Series A and B and almost failed to raise the C; every objection ('what if Google does this', 'no one will grant location permissions') became something to answer next time.

ideas.idea: Investor objections become a feature map: track the questions people ask and come back with one-two-three reasons each is solved.
ideas.detail: Cherie adds that a friend pitched about 30 VCs while not raising, wrote down every question, and later closed a seed round with a tight argument; she plans to do the same for Sisters Worldwide.

ideas.idea: Competition can be good for a novel business because competitors do the market education for you.
ideas.detail: Read AI grew 10x on Microsoft in the year after Copilot launched; Cherie saw the same when TikTok launched AR ads competing with Snapchat's, and the sisters see it with Starbucks matcha helping Sisters Matcha, though low-quality cafe matcha also forces re-education.

ideas.idea: In a high-stakes meeting, focus only on delivering what you came to communicate and don't try to predict their reaction.
ideas.detail: David used to overthink scenarios; now he asks 'what am I in this meeting for' and delivers the value proposition, because worrying about reactions throws you off.

ideas.idea: If you're solving a real problem, a flubbed pitch doesn't matter; the product speaks for itself.
ideas.detail: When Snap's Imran Khan asked what he'd do with Snapchat big-picture, David gave a narrow answer about measuring store visits; Imran later called it 'the worst answer ever', yet Snapchat acquired Placed a couple of quarters later.

ideas.idea: VCs get pitched so often they will forget a bad first pitch, so let rejection wash off and come back with a second, better pitch.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Cherie relates that Goldman Sachs rejected her twice for internships in 2008 and 2009 before hiring her on the third try with a completely new set of interviewers; being forgotten worked in her favor.

ideas.idea: Meeting notes will become a commodity; AI is moving from assistant to agent to optimization of outcomes across all channels.
ideas.detail: Like ad tech unifying exposures and conversions, combining meetings, messages, calls and emails lets AI say '12 clients complained about this feature, want me to draft a PRD?'; Read AI's roadmap includes a Chrome extension summarizing email and auto-complete that fills answers from your meetings.

ideas.idea: Don't practice in the hour or two before a speech; do the prep earlier and let your brain process it in the background so you can respond to the room.
ideas.detail: At a recent talk David saw 75% of the audience on their phones during the prior speaker and changed his opening on the spot, which was only possible because he knew his tenets and wasn't locked to scripted lines.

ideas.idea: Great public speakers are made through reps: 100-200 startup pitch competitions turned speaking into second nature.
ideas.detail: Early on David spoke to four or five people at bad conferences, which was freeing because 'what's the worst that can happen'; the sisters add that their best-speaking friends did debate or model Congress, learning to argue ideas without taking it personally.

ideas.idea: You can judge a conference's content quality by how many laptops and phones are open in the audience.
ideas.detail: At this conference people were engaged, raising hands, staying for sessions and trying to meet each other rather than sell.

ideas.idea: The way to start anything is to just start; the first few attempts will be questionable quality but that's how you learn.
ideas.detail: Jean answers the frequent question 'how did you make a podcast' by saying you minimize time-to-start and use the resources available, as David did with the library printer.

ideas.idea: Doubt and hard questions from others are more useful than silence because they tell you exactly what to address next time.
ideas.detail: The sisters note that pushback without crashing out is part of entrepreneurial resilience; getting nothing back means you were 'just practicing talking'.

ideas.idea: Water off a duck's back: positive and negative feedback should affect you the same way; don't react too high to highs or too low to lows.
ideas.detail: Cherie's former boss Eric Wollenbacher taught this equilibrium mindset, which mirrors David's 'let it wash off you'.

ideas.idea: DILMO: Do It, Learn, Move On, an acronym Cherie coined in 2021 for letting go after action.
ideas.detail: Cherie says moving on is the hardest part and she has been trying to make DILMO happen for years, including in a TikTok.

ideas.idea: Product education and changing user behavior is the hardest part of a launch, so competitors doing that work with you cuts your job in half.
ideas.detail: Building Snapchat's AR advertising platform, Cherie had to explain, demo, prove efficacy and then sell each advertiser; TikTok entering meant Coca-Cola and Pizza Hut had already heard the pitch.
